subject: chemistry-1
question: Fluorine (F2) is a gas at room temperature while iodine (I2) is a solid, even though both are nonpolar diatomic molecules. Which comparison is accurate?

options.text: Iodine molecules are polar and fluorine molecules are not, so iodine has dipole-dipole forces.
Iodine molecules hydrogen bond to one another, which fluorine molecules cannot do.
Iodine has far more electrons in a larger, more polarizable cloud, so dispersion is stronger.
Fluorine is more electronegative, so fluorine molecules attract one another more strongly.

explanation:
Both molecules are homonuclear, so neither has a permanent dipole and dispersion is the only force available to either. Dispersion strength tracks polarizability, which rises with the number of electrons and how loosely the outer ones are held: I2 carries 106 electrons versus 18 for F2, a difference of 88. Iodine's large, easily distorted cloud produces attractions strong enough to hold a crystalline solid melting at 113.7 degrees Celsius, while F2 boils at -188 degrees Celsius. Note that electronegativity describes electron pull within a bond, not attraction between separate molecules.

ELI-10: Dispersion depends on how easily an electron cloud can be pushed out of shape, and big loose clouds distort far more than small tight ones. Fluorine's eighteen electrons are held close to two small nuclei, so its momentary dipoles are tiny and the molecules barely stick. Iodine's one hundred six electrons sit in large outer shells that shift easily, producing much stronger momentary dipoles. More electrons and greater volume mean stronger dispersion, which is the usual reason substances get less volatile as you move down a group.
